An energy declaration (in Swedish, “energideklaration”) is an official report—often called an Energy Performance Certificate (EPC)—that summarizes a building’s actual or calculated energy use, rates its energy efficiency and suggests cost-effective measures for improvement. In Sweden the requirement stems from the EU’s Energy Performance of Buildings Directive and is administered by Boverket (the National Board of Housing, Building and Planning).

Key features of an energy declaration include:
•	A measured or calculated annual energy use (expressed in kWh/m²)  
•	An energy-efficiency class, typically graded from A (best) to G (worst)  
•	Information on the building’s heated floor area (Atemp), number of floors, number of stairwells, construction type and other physical characteristics  
•	Recommendations for upgrades (e.g. improved insulation, window replacement, heating system optimization) with estimated energy and cost savings  
•	Validity of 10 years, after which a new declaration

Energy-efficiency improvement refers to any set of technical or structural measures that lowers a building’s energy use per square meter of heated floor area (Atemp) and thus raises its energy performance certification (epc_egienergiklass). In other words, you carry out interventions—such as adding or upgrading insulation, installing high-performance windows, optimizing heating and ventilation systems (for example with heat-recovery units), switching to LED lighting or more efficient appliances, and implementing smart controls—that reduce annual energy demand (kWh/m²).  

By reducing energy consumption in relation to the building’s size, these measures:

• Improve the EPC class (from G up toward A on Sweden’s A–G scale)  
• Cut operating costs and energy bills  
• Enhance indoor comfort (more stable temperatures, better air quality)  
• Lower greenhouse-gas emissions

In the electric-vehicle industry there is no single, legally binding “line” between normal and fast charging, but the following brackets are widely used in Europe (and increasingly elsewhere) as conventions:

1.  AC (alternating-current) charging  
   • Slow charging: up to about 3.7 kW (typical home socket or basic wall-box)  
   • Medium charging: 3.7 – 22 kW (dedicated home/business chargers or small public stations)  
   • Fast AC charging: above 22 kW (often found at public on-street or commercial sites)  

2.  DC (direct-current) charging  
   • Rapid (or “DC fast”) charging: typically 50 – 150 kW  
   • Ultra-fast charging: above 150 kW  

By these market conventions, the most common “boundary” between what people call normal (slow or medium AC) and fast charging is around 22 kW for AC chargers. In the DC realm, charging powers of 50 kW or higher are generally classified as fast (or rapid) charging.

   • Standard: SS-EN 1838 “Application of lighting for emergency situations.”  
   • Requirement: Minimum 1 lux at floor level along the center line of the escape route (including stairs), so that occupants can see and follow the evacuation path in case of normal‐power failure.

According to Sweden’s national building regulations (Boverkets byggregler, BBR), indoor‐climate requirements in Chapter 8 (“Hälso‐ och hygienkrav”) only apply to rooms where people normally stay (“uppehållsutrymmen”) – living rooms, bedrooms, kitchens, sanitary rooms etc. A stairwell is not classed as an uppehållsrum and is therefore not assigned a mandatory minimum temperature in BBR.  

That said, in practice property owners and managers will typically:

• Ensure the stairwell stays above about +10 °C to  
  – prevent frost damage to building components  
  – avoid condensation and mold risk  
• If the stairwell doubles as an evacuation waiting area (tillfällig vistelse före utrymning), some designers choose to maintain at least +12 to +16 °C for occupant comfort  

But to be clear:  
– No explicit “must-have” temperature for stairwells is stated in BBR.  
– Any heating-level decision should be guided by moisture control, frost protection and, if relevant, user comfort standards.
